div.p: Real-time system is said to be failed in case it is unable to produce response at correct time. Networked based real-time systems are much more prone to this kind of failures. Dependability model only consider hardware failures. For timeliness (ability to produce response at correct time), only worst-case guarantee is used. The paper proposes a method to derive timeliness hazard rate. This will enable in deriving a single dependability model of system with hardware and timeliness failures.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In real-time systems, missing deadline is as dangerous as producing incorrect response (i.e. value). So, real-time system failure has two causes, i) value, and ii) failing to produce response at correct time (i.e. timeliness). A real-time system using shared communication network for performing its function is called a networked real-time (NRT) system.

With the advancement of networking technology, it is penetrating into application area requiring real-time responses. This is due to the enormous advantage -modularity, decentralization of control, integrated diagnosis, quick and easy maintenance and low cost -these systems offer. Ensuring timing characteristic becomes much more important for networked based real-time systems.

Most dependability models do not consider timeliness failure. To guarantee timeliness, worst-case analysis is used in literature. Worst-case analysis is a deterministic method to guarantee response-time, while for hardware, probabilistic methods are used. In addition to other drawbacks of this analysis, one has to analyze failures affecting both value and timeliness separately. This makes the decision process difficult. A probabilistic measure for timeliness and its incorporation in dependability models could solve this problem by providing a single dependability measure [13].

In this paper, an analytical method to model effect of network and node redundancies on system response-time is proposed. The system response-time distribution is used to predict system timeliness. Then a method is proposed to estimate timeliness hazard rate. These methods are proposed with reference to CAN [2,3,13] and MIL-STD-1553B [14,13] although these can be extended other networks also.

Section II gives a brief introduction to response-time model available in literature. Effect of network and node redundancy is modeled in section III and IV respectively. System response time is discussed in section V. Dependence of response-time in consecutive cycle is modeled in section VI and modeling of timeliness hazard rate is discussed in section VII. Finally conclusions are given in section VIII.

div.head: II. RESPONSE TIME MODELS
div.p: Real-time communication aims at providing timely and deterministic data exchange between devices. A number of technologies are available now days. These are based on Medium Access Control (MAC) protocols such as random access protocols (CSMNCD, CSMNCA, CSMNCR), fixed assignment protocols (TDMA), and demand assignment protocols (token based). Examples of these are Ethernet (also CAN), MIL-STD-1553B and token bus respectively.

In some cases, response-time may be deterministic (MIL-STD-1553B), while in cases it is very difficult (CAN, Ethernet). A number of literatures are available on estimation of response time of various networks [1-6, 13, 15]. The methods vary from analytical/simulation model to base on measurement. This paper assumes the response-time model of the network is available. It models the effect of network and node redundancies on overall system response-time. Based on this, a method is proposed to derive timeliness hazard rate.

div.head: III. EFFECT OF NETWORK REDUNDANCY
div.p: In this section effect of hot network redundancy on network delay is analyzed. Hot network redundancy means, all redundant channels are working simultaneously. Let n number of independent networks connects all the nodes. All nodes have independent network interface units (NID) for each network. A node after computation put the data for transmission on all the NIDs simultaneously. NIUs independently transfer the data on their respective networks. To analyze effect of network redundancy, two networks -random access based, time division multiple access based -CAN and MIL-STD-1553B are taken. Response-time models of these are discussed in . It only has message identifier, which is used to assign priority to message and receiving nodes use this for filtering relevant message for them. A typical diagram of a node with multiple CAN networks is shown in Fig. 1. Node NIDs does not perform any computation except framing whose delay time can be neglected. With the assumption that every node put their data to all Nill s simultaneously, and under condition that CAN bus utilization is <1, all redundant network channels will work in perfect synchronization. So, redundancy at CAN network level does not affect network delay. It only provides fault tolerance against failure of any network channel andior NID.

div.head: VI. DEPENDENCE OF RESPONSE-TIME BETWEEN CONSECUTIVE CYCLES
div.p: In the above analysis, we considered that nodes are asynchronous. The analysis is valid only for initial or first response, as nodes and network controllers are carryin g out their periodically. Local clocks of nodes as well as network controllers (if any) are very stable. So, if system response-time is, x at first cycle after startup, chances are very high that it will remain x in consecutive cycle( s). Response-times of consecutive cycles are correlated. From common logic it can be inferred, any variation in consecutive response-times will be due to drift in clocks, failure of node/controller and restoration of node/controller.
A networked real-time system, able to meets its deadline at startup may fail after operating for time t, due to drift in clocks, failure and restoration of nodes/network controllers.

div.head: A. CAN
div.p: Network delay on CAN has variation mainly due to traffic and priority among messages. Message with lower priority has higher variation than high priority messages. Network delay of a message in one cycle is not related with the delay in the previous cycle, as the interacting traffic is independent. So, network delay in each cycle is independent.

div.head: B. MIL-STD-1553B
div.p: As discussed earlier, network delay in case of MIL-STD-1553B has variation mainly because of mismatch in clocks of remote terminals and bus controllers. Most of the cases, this mismatch is very small. So, network delay in consecutive cycles will have small variations, means network delay is dependent on previous cycle. Let network delay of data from node A to B is measured in cycle k, and then network delay in cycle k+ 1 is going to be around the measured value with a high probability. Although network response-time at any random cycle will follow the pdf given in [13][14], but network delay in consecutive cycle will be dependent on current cycle network delay.

div.head: VII. MODELING OF TIMELINESS HAzARD RATE
div.p: Systems usually have robust control algorithm to tolerate message delays and drops. Message delay and drop has effect of delaying control action by networked real-time systems. Delay beyond a specified time in taking control action is considered timeliness failure.

Let system failure criteria is n consecutive deadline violation (or timeliness failures). When n=l, number of cycles at which timeliness failure will occur follows geometric distribution. (16) Geometric distribution is a memory less distribution in discrete time and is counterpart of exponential distribution in continuous time. At gross level (larger time scale), it can be easily converted to exponential distribution. In exponential distribution characterizing parameter is hazard rate, which in this case is referred to as "timeliness hazard rate".
Where "AT stands for timeliness hazard rate, t for operating time and te for cycle time.

When n > 1, number of cycles for timeliness failure will not follow geometric distribution. This process (number of cycles for timeliness failure) is a memory process and directly cannot be modeled as Markov. Using the technique of additional states [10], Markov model can be used to model this process. A DTMC (Discrete Time Markov Chain) for this process is shown in Figure 5.n is clear a general equation for n cannot be given. This gives rise to computational problem for higher values of n. Also, it will be better if this process can be mapped to a continuous time process, as it will enable modeling of timeliness failure along with hardware failures in system dependability modeling.
One algorithm to evaluate timeliness hazard is by using (17). Alternate method to estimate hazard rate is by its definition.

div.head: A. Example
div.p: Consider a two node system with 3 networks interconnecting them. One node acts as sensor & controller (SC) node and other node acts as actuator (A) node. Interconnecting network system is taken to be CAN (case I) in one case and MIL-STD-1553B (case II) in the other.

System components may fail and restored back by means of repair. In degraded states (system has some faulty components, but still system is functional) response time change. In all working states system's response-time is computed using method discussed in this paper.

Messages with 2 bytes and 10ms cycle time are considered for both the cases. On network other messages are taken. System has total ofl7 [13,16]. Messages for present case I, have message ID 8,9 and 12 (with message ID 12 having 10ms as period). For case I, 4 healthy and degraded states are considered [13].

In case of CAN bus, redundancy at CAN level does not affect the system response-time, while in case of MIL-STD-1553B, failure of network channels do affect the system response-time. For case II, 10 healthy and degraded states are considered [13].

div.head: ACKNOWLEDGMENTS
div.p: The authors would like to thank Prof. Varsha Apte (IITB) for reviewing the initial work and guidance to make this work possible. We also thanks Shri P.P. Marathe and Shri M.K. Singh (both from BARC) for their continual support and encouragement during the work.

VIII. CONCLUSIONS Network-induced delays are important for NRT systems as they are the cause of system degradation, failure and sometime system's stability. NRT system's control algorithms considering probabilistic network delay have better control Quality of Performance (QoP). In this paper, method to estimate timeliness hazard rate is proposed. Effect of network redundancy on system response-time for CAN and MIL-STD-1553B networks is analyzed. The method is extended to evaluate sample-to actuation delay and response-time. A fault-tolerant NRT system has a number of nodes within sensor, controller and actuator groups, effect to these redundancies on system response-time is also analyzed. Assuming probability of missing deadline in each cycle is constant and given failure criteria, a method to derive timeliness hazard rate is given. This method derives hazard rate from a discrete time process. This timeliness hazard rate can be used to derive homogenous dependability models. These homogenous dependability models consider hardware failures by means of hardware hazard rate and timeliness failure by means of timeliness hazard rate.
